stances.claim: The main duty of every director -- including the Independent Director -- is fidelity to the corporation itself, above the pecuniary wants of any shareholder and beyond the ID's own personal interests; the conventional view that the ID represents minority shareholders is misplaced.
stances.rhetorical_move: thesis-correction (replacing the conventional answer with a principled answer)

stances.claim: What makes IDs different is their independence from any shareholder, and as such, their owed loyalty is only to the law and to the ideals of good corporate governance -- uphold truth, fairness, transparency, accountability.
stances.rhetorical_move: differentia-specifica framing (defining the role by what makes it independent)

stances.claim: Sustained productive engagement at age 83 with multiple boards is possible only through a four-criteria personal framework: comfort with major shareholders, no rivalry conflicts, deep business study, and ruthless time-management with near-100% attendance.
stances.rhetorical_move: personal-praxis disclosure (modeling the work ethic he prescribes)

stances.claim: Productivity and discipline are not incompatible with happiness: 'Believe it or not, I am happy when I am overworked' -- and the SC tenure's record output (most decisions, one book per year, no backlog) is offered as living proof.
stances.rhetorical_move: happiness-through-discipline framing (with self-quoted Carpio endorsement as third-party validation)

notable_anecdotes: The Carpio quote -- 'CJ Panganiban is the most prolific writer of the Court, bar none' -- deployed as third-party validation of CJ's productivity claim; notable because Carpio and CJ are well-known for disagreeing on substantive doctrine but here Carpio underwrites CJ's work-output reputation.

The book-per-year claim during his SC term -- CJ explicitly notes 'no other justice in the Court's 118-year history has written one book a year in addition to producing the most number of decisions,' the most historicized productivity boast in his writing.
The uninterrupted Sunday column streak from Feb 11, 2007 -- invoked as one of CJ's two parallel disciplined output records (SC tenure + Inquirer column).
The geographic concentration of CJ's board meetings (Makati/Taguig/Pasig -- all reachable from his Makati residence) -- quietly disclosed as the operational secret behind 100% attendance.

The closing valedictory -- 'within the time and space the Good Lord would allow me, before calling me to an even more glorious world in the Great Beyond' -- one of CJ's most explicit late-life mortality acknowledgments framed in faith language.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with the new Revised Corporation Code's (RA 11232) legalistic definition of Independent Directors as those independent of management and free from materially-interfering relationships, then notes the law does not enumerate their duties. Asked what their main duty is, he answers: fidelity to the corporation -- above the pecuniary wants of any shareholder, and beyond the ID's own personal interests. 'With due respect' to those who believe IDs represent the minority, he argues IDs owe loyalty only to the law and to the ideals of good corporate governance: truth, fairness, transparency, accountability. He then explains how, at age 83, he meets the demands of multiple board posts and foundation trusteeships via four criteria -- join only where comfortable with the major shareholders and corporate culture; decline rivalrous conflicts (or accept only with both friend-rivals' permission); study the business deeply enough to surface related-party transactions and irregularities; and impose ruthless time management with near-100% meeting attendance, helped by advance scheduling and the geographic concentration of his Makati/Taguig/Pasig boards. He recalls his SC work habits -- bringing work home, reading pleadings nights and weekends -- and, 'modesty aside,' notes he produced the most decisions in 11+ years on the Court, with one book per year and no backlog at retirement -- a record no other justice in 118 years has matched. He quotes Antonio T. Carpio: 'CJ Panganiban is the most prolific writer of the Court, bar none.' He confesses to being 'a glutton for work,' happy when overworked, and notes the Sunday column streak uninterrupted since Feb 11, 2007. He closes valedictorily, observing that his 12+ post-judicial years have now exceeded his 11+ years on the Court, and pledges to keep working as hard and happy as long as the Good Lord allows, 'before calling me to an even more glorious world in the Great Beyond.'
